amstar2_items.justification: Research questions and eligibility criteria do not follow PICO components; instead, the review poses four broad conceptual and thematic mapping questions regarding the meaning of water justice, its relationship to SDG 6, geographic/thematic concentrations, and proposed solutions.

The authors cite a protocol published in the Australian National University Open Repository (Fanaian 2024) documenting selection criteria and coding rules and describe iterative pilot refinement on 20 articles plus a post-protocol March 2024 follow-up search for 2023 papers, but the protocol was published in 2024 after/during screening of the 2012–2022 corpus and lacked a pre-specified risk-of-bias or quantitative synthesis plan.

The review pooled peer-reviewed journal articles, book chapters, and secondary reviews (both theoretical essays and empirical case studies) while excluding gray literature and monographs, without providing a methodological justification for combining these heterogeneous publication types.

Six databases (Scopus, Web of Science, Science Direct, Springer, JSTOR Constellate, and Google Scholar) were searched with reported search terms ("water justice" OR "water equity") and discussed restrictions (English-only, 2012–2023), satisfying Partial Yes, but the narrow two-phrase query excluded related terms ("human right to water", "water access") and omitted gray literature, reference-list chasing, and trial/study registries.

Three co-authors manually screened titles and abstracts with discrepancies resolved via peer validation and expert input, and full-text exclusion decisions during coding were cross-checked by three researchers and expert input.

Although the deductive coding framework was piloted on 20 articles and two researchers "collaborated on the full-text review and literature coding," independent duplicate data extraction with consensus or inter-rater reliability verification across the 470 included records is not demonstrated.

Aggregate counts and reasons for the 72 full-text exclusions are reported in Section 2.4 (insufficient engagement n=28, duplicates n=7, gray literature n=2, unavailability n=35), and Figure 1 renders as a blank image in the PDF, with no bibliographic list of excluded full-text studies provided.

No study-by-study characteristics table (detailing populations, interventions/exposures, methods, outcomes, and settings of the 470 included publications) is provided in the article text, and the Data Availability Statement notes no dataset is shared; Supporting Information Annex Tables 1–5 contain aggregate country counts, SDG keyword mappings, solution theme terms, and justice definitions rather than individual study profiles.
No risk-of-bias or critical appraisal tool was applied to evaluate the methodological quality of any of the 470 included publications.
Sources of funding for the 470 individual publications included in the review were neither extracted nor reported.
No quantitative meta-analysis was performed; synthesis relied on deductive qualitative coding and descriptive bibliometric/thematic counts.

Because study-level risk of bias or empirical rigor was never assessed, methodological quality was not accounted for in interpreting findings, aside from a brief caveat that many proposed solutions in the literature are untested recommendations.

The authors extensively examine and explain conceptual, geographic (Global South vs. Global North), scalar (local, national, transboundary, global), and temporal (2012–2014, 2015–2019, 2020–2023) heterogeneity across the reviewed scholarship.
No quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis was conducted.
Funding sources (Hilda John Endowment at ANU, ARC Laureate Fellowship FL190100164, and IWMI support) and a declaration of no conflicts of interest are explicitly reported.

raw_response.methodological_notes: Fanaian et al. (2025) is classified under WIREs Water's "SYSTEMATIC REVIEW" rubric and follows PRISMA 2020 screening mechanics across six databases (2299 records -> 1935 deduplicated abstracts -> 542 full texts -> 470 included publications; protocol published in ANU Open Repository as Fanaian 2024). Methodologically, however, it functions as a broad systematic scoping/thematic mapping review rather than an empirical effectiveness review: (1) its search string was strictly limited to "water justice" OR "water equity" and explicitly excluded studies framed solely around "human right to water" or "water access"; (2) its 470-item corpus pools primary empirical studies alongside theoretical essays, edited-volume chapters, and other secondary reviews (e.g., De Guzman et al. 2023; Leonard et al. 2023; Schmidt 2023; Zuniga-Teran et al. 2021; Rusca and Cleaver 2022; Gupta et al. 2022a/b — omitted from included_primary_studies above to avoid review-on-review conflation); (3) no individual study table or bibliography of the 470 included records is printed in the PDF or shared as open data ("Data sharing is not applicable"), and Annex Tables 1–5 in Supporting Information contain only thematic/country aggregations; and (4) no risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, yielding Critically Low confidence under AMSTAR 2 (critical flaws on Q7, Q9, and Q13). Narrow Criterion 2 is borderline because a substantive subset of synthesized primary studies examines legal, regulatory, tariff, shutoff, ownership, and slum-tenure WASH rules (e.g., Bae et al. 2023 on SDWA enforcement; Stewart 2022 on mandatory consolidation; Lubeck-Schricker et al. 2023 on legal exclusion in Mumbai slums; Zhang et al. 2022a/b on public vs. private water pricing and shutoff moratoria), whereas the overall corpus spans river basins, irrigation, hydropower, lithium mining, tourism, and non-empirical theory.
raw_response.review_design_self_description: systematic review (PRISMA 2020 deductive qualitative and bibliometric thematic review of 470 journal articles, book chapters, and reviews)
